#36. 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire

Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired?

Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?

We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates, external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.

But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?

Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager.

He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI.

"Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."

Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicants

While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.

He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates.

"That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."

This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI "at some stages of the recruitment process".

According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.

However, it also found 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.

On top of this, the tech is helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.

EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employees

Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.

EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but decided to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.

Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process.

"What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."

Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible.

It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates.

But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews.

"A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script."

AI job application rise 'risks hiring incapable staff'

AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analysts

Young jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AI

One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews.

While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would.

"I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"

According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.

And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI in the recruitment process, 29% plan to introduce it within the next year.

Hollie Moody says EDF does not currently use AI in its recruitment process but may have to in future.

For her, the use of AI in job applications remains a "moral dilemma" that employers and candidates will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits.

"It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."

Have you used AI to apply for a job or are you an employer who uses AI to find the best candidate? Share your experiences

Correction 14 October: This article has been amended to show that according to the ISE's survey 29% of employers plan to introduce AI in the recruitment process over the next year, rather than more than half as we originally reported.

#37. How long will humans be needed for translation?

Google's translation service handles one trillion words per month

"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating, external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation, external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

AI translation is the "right call" in many cases says Jonathan Zimmermann

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says Jonathan Zimmermann, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmermann.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Ariella Baltié specialises in legal translation work

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

Carol Bereuter is a specialist in medical translations

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.

He thinks a new generation of tech will be an improvement.

"We will see translation systems that are increasingly capable of evaluating what they do and correcting themselves using different AI tools simultaneously: one to do the translation, a second to criticize it and a third to produce a new version, for example."

But perhaps the big moment will be when AI can show doubt.

"The real breakthrough won't come until these systems are not merely capable of translating but also of telling us when they're not sure," Yvon says.

#38. Bumble bought for $1.3bn in 'bet on the future of humanity'

Dating app Bumble has been bought for $1.3bn (£980m) in what the new owners called "a bet on the future of humanity".

Investment firm Ithaca Holdings is taking over the loss-making firm and it directors, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will become co-chief executives of the company which once differentiated itself by having a "women-first" chat rule.

Bumble ditched the rule in August this year.

Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble's founder and current chief executive, said she would remain "actively involved" with the business she set up 12 years ago.

While it is unclear what Wolfe Herd's role at the dating app will be, she said she will work closely with the new owners.

Gupta and Hegeman said they wanted to use technology to "renew and accelerate businesses...in a world transformed by AI".

They said: "Technology should work in service of our deepest source of fulfillment, human connection and this investment is a bet on the future of humanity."

This contrasts with a recent debate over the safety of AI, with some experts claiming the speed of its development threatens the future of humanity.

Bumble's share price has soared as news of the deal began to emerge. The jump lifted its company valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after it floated the business on the Nasdaq stock index in 2021.

Since becoming a public company, it has made an annual pre-tax profit only once, in 2023.

In the following two years, it reported steep losses, though during that period Bumble had been working to incorporate new technology, including AI, into its app.

Its chief executive in 2024, Lidiane Jones, told the BBC she believed AI had "exciting potential" in dating apps related to safety, and Bumble had been looking at research that found Gen Z and milliennials were interested in AI assistance with creating profiles.

This year, the dating app unveiled several new AI features, including profile guidance to help people create dating profiles.

Bumble was launched in 2014 by Wolfe Herd who built the brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches.

It recently abandoned that rule, prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals.

"Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August.

Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates.

Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating.

Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services.

Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021.

According to a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier.

Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers, book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner.

I've seen her name and photo - but we can't talk before the date. Will it work out?

#39. Phase Eight and Hobbs owner hit by cyber-attack, as H&M probes separate hack claim

The owner of high-end fashion brands Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight says it is investigating a cyber-security incident.

According to TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - it identified an incident on Sunday affecting some IT systems and "specifically impacting our Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles brands".

"We are actively investigating and working with external cyber security specialists," the company told BBC News in a statement.

Meanwhile, H&M is investigating a separate claim that it was attacked by a notorious hacking group.

TFG said its brands' stores are operating as normal but some website capabilities may be unavailable, adding "we apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate".

The retail group reportedly told customers in an email that it did not believe customers' payment information had been affected by the incident.

"As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted," it said.

The email, seen by news service PA, also said that those whose personal information had been impacted would be informed directly.

"We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time," it added.

Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Bucks New University told PA that this was "a clear sign that major brands are firmly in the crosshairs of cyber attackers".

Fashion giants ranging from Adidas to Alexander McQueen have been targeted by cyber-criminals seeking to extort money by threatening to release customer data unless they are paid a ransom.

"No organisation is immune, so the real test of resilience is how quickly a business can detect an incident, respond and recover while keeping its customers informed," Griffiths said - adding customers should stay "vigilant" and wary of suspicious messages.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, said attacks targeting retailers were "starting to look rather like buses... you wait for one, and suddenly three come along at once".

She told the BBC that while it was too soon to ascertain how the incident affecting TFG London's systems occurred, or whether it was related to other recent hacks, "the retail industry has some serious questions to answer about how exposed its systems have become".

On Monday, it was also reported that fashion giant H&M was investigating a claim of a hack by a cyber-criminal group called ShinyHunters.

The hackers have been previously linked to high-profile attacks including targeting the FBI, Rockstar Games and Ticketmaster.

"We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims," H&M told BBC News in a statement.

"At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised."

It also comes only a week after Asos customers were informed the online fashion and beauty retailer had been hacked by another group, via a push notification appearing on their phone screens.

Cyber-security experts told the BBC it was an unprecedented move for hackers to effectively transform an app notification system into a "ransom note".

It later emerged that hackers had obtained more detailed personal information belonging to Asos customers than the retailer initially suggested.

An update was issued to customers after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said the breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

#48. Fast-moving California wildfire burns homes as people are ordered to leave

Watch: Aircraft deployed to fight burning Bryson fire in Malibu

Evacuation orders in California are in effect due to a rapidly growing wildfire that has already burned six homes south of Los Angeles.

The Norte Fire erupted on Friday in Orange County and quickly grew to 465 acres by the evening. By Saturday morning, it spread to 570 acres (2.3 sq km), with 5% containment.

One firefighter suffered heat exhaustion while battling the blaze.

Officials say the fierce Santa Ana winds will blow until Saturday, bringing further risk of more conflagrations.

The US National Weather Service (NWS) has issued a red flag warning for several California counties due to strong, gusty winds combined with low humidity and dry vegetation that create critical wildfire spread conditions.

The Norte Fire is one of 10 burning across the state, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.

In an update on Friday evening, Division 3 Fire Chief Mark Backoff said that six homes had either been damaged or destroyed by the Norte Fire, and one firefighter had been injured from heat exhaustion.

"We continue to engage in the firefight, and have additional resources coming," he said.

Footage posted online showed blazes tearing through homes in the communities of San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano.

The Bryson Fire, burning in the affluent coastal city of Malibu in Los Angeles county, has also sparked evacuation orders throughout the Santa Monica mountains and has grown to 147 acres, with 52% of the blaze contained.

More than 400 firefighters have been fighting the blaze.

Watch: Smoke towers over California neighbourhood as wildfire burns homes

Further south, the Henderson Fire in San Diego county erupted on Thursday, and has grown to over 3,100 acres (12.5 sq km), including around Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, with about 35% contained as of Saturday morning.

The size of the blaze has twice forced officials to close the I-5 highway, an important route that runs the length of the US West Coast.

The fires are being fanned by the Santa Ana winds, which normally begin during cooler months from late September to May.

Officials say the winds peaked on Friday, but will remain dangerous into early Saturday morning.

Six homes have been damaged or destroyed in Orange County

Winds topped 40mph (64km/h) in the Los Angeles area, the NWS said, adding that motorists should watch for debris blown into roadways.

Temperatures were far above average for this time of year in southern California, further driving up the fire danger.

The NWS has issued a heat advisory, saying that the danger of heat-related illness remained high.

Forecasts expect temperatures to reach 95F (35C) in southern California on Saturday.

#49. Avian flu and costs among reasons for loss of captive birds at Castle Espie

Bird migration is a visible annual event at Castle Espie

Avian flu, cost-cutting and Brexit are among the reasons behind the transfer of captive birds from one of Northern Ireland's best-known wildlife sites, according to the charity that runs it.

Director of Operations at Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) Alex Lane said avian influenza, as well as difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit, has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds at Castle Espie.

The closure of both the site's captive bird programme and guided school tour programme is part of wider WWT cost-cutting measures.

An Assembly member has described the changes to the education offering as "disappointing".

Alex Lane said the site used to have around 500 birds in its captive collection - but, a combination of Brexit and avian influenza means today, there are fewer than 100.

Both the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs and the UK's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs have been contacted for comment.

From November onwards, all captive birds at Castle Espie will be transferred to other WWT sites across the UK.

The centre, which is located in County Down, will also no longer offer guided school tours.

However, the centre have said they will "continue to welcome self-guided school visits".

The centre has different types of wetlands

Castle Espie, which is managed by the WWT, is located on the shores of Strangford Lough, just outside Comber.

The reserve is a safe haven for native and exotic birds, ducks and geese, and some of its collection including globally at-risk species.

It has different types of wetlands, including freshwater and sailing lagoons as well as seasonally flooded areas.

Cara Hunter said the "loss of guided educational visits is disappointing"

SDLP MLA Cara Hunter, who sits on the Stormont education committee, told BBC News NI that the "loss of guided educational visits is disappointing".

"Castle Espie has played an important role in introducing generations of young people to nature, conservation and the unique environment on their doorstep.

"I would be concerned that these changes could reduce opportunities for schools, particularly those with limited resources, to access high-quality environmental education."

The MLA added that "opportunities that educate, inspire and broaden horizons are quietly lost while Stormont remains distracted from the issues that matter most to families".

Captive mallards at the Castle Espie site

Castle Espie will cease to offer its formal education offer

Alex Lane, Director of Operations at WWT, said rising costs and the challenge around income means charities like the WWT are facing "increasing pressure".

"We've got a sizeable deficit and obviously that's unsustainable in the long term," she told BBC News NI.

Lane said it is important the WWT have surplus income so that they can "do the conservation work that is part of their mission".

She said the site used to have over 500 birds in its captive collection - but, in part due to avian influenza, today there are less than 100.

The reserve is a safe haven for native and exotic birds

Lane added that another factor in the decline in the number of captive birds is the increased difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit.

"There is no aligned system for bringing birds into Ireland from mainland UK.

"We've got a vastly reduced collection, and that's not by choice. That is the impact of avian influenza and the restrictions placed on bird movement as a result of Brexit."

It is thought that diverging post-Brexit bio-security checks has increased red tape for moving birds between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

Under the strict mandates of the Windsor Framework, these regulatory shifts also mean heavy administrative and logistical costs.

According to the UK Government's official website, external, the movement of captive birds from Britain to Northern Ireland requires an export health certificate.

There is also a requirement for captive birds to be checked at the point of entry when transported to Northern Ireland, to protect animal health and welfare and public health.

However, Lane said there will be benefits to the decommissioning of the captive bird collection.

"The intent with the site is to reset it as this hub for wetland nature conservation.

"We're effectively opening up more space for wild birds."

Lane said the site "needs to stop" its formal education offering in part due to financial pressures WWT faces.

She added that there is also an insufficient number of schools booking guided tours at the site to cover costs.

Lane said the low number of school visits may be partly be caused by the cost of transport.

#50. Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?

With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.

Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.

This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.

However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El Niño strengthens in the Pacific.

As autumn sets in and the nights get longer temperatures around polar regions start to fall. This causes a greater contrast with the warmer tropics which can fire up a more potent jet stream - the fast moving, narrow band of fast winds high in the atmosphere.

The jet stream is largely responsible for developing and delivering our stormier pressure systems.

Typically in autumn the jet stream would be a regular visitor to the skies above the UK, steering wet and windy weather towards us.

However, so far this season it has often been sitting to the north or north-west of the UK. This has meant south or south-westerly winds bringing warmer than normal conditions and high pressure having more of an influence leading to reduced rainfall for many.

So far this autumn the jet stream has been largely to the north-west of the UK, steering stormy low pressure systems away

These weather patterns have therefore meant only occasional bouts of stronger winds across the north-west of the UK, with little disruption.

The heaviest of the rain has also been focused across Scotland and Northern Ireland while parts of England and Wales have continued to be much drier than normal.

Parts of Herefordshire for instance have only received a tenth of the rainfall they would normally have seen by mid-October so far this month.

Some of the biggest impacts of the dry weather have been across the southern England where exceptionally low reservoir levels have prompted the Environment Agency to declare "severe drought" in some areas.

Is there a hosepipe ban in my area? What you need to know

A change in the position of that jet stream and its strength is expected through the coming week.

This will allow deeper low pressure systems to affect more parts of the UK marking a shift to a more widespread wetter and windier weather.

Forecasts will need to be monitored closely as there is potential later in the week that we could see our first spell of widely disruptive weather this season.

There are also longer term signals for increased rainfall and storminess later in autumn and early winter in the UK.

The Met Office's current three month outlook covering October, November and December forecasts a double the normal chance of wetter weather and 1.3 times the normal chance of windier weather which is consistent with the type of patterns seen with previous El Niño events.

Storms are most often named when potentially damaging winds are forecast, but can also be named for flooding rain or disruptive snow.

They were first named to help bring public attention to episodes of severe weather, to help people prepare to avoid the worst impacts by planning ahead.

In Europe, there are five storm naming groups created from the meteorological agencies based in a similar geographic location.

The UK, Ireland, and the Netherlands form the western storm-naming group which started naming storms in 2015.

Weather systems are named by the the UK's Met Office, Ireland's Met Éireann and Netherland's KNMI based on expected weather impacts as well as how likely those are.

The winter months of December, January and February typically produce the highest number of UK storms

Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer. The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK, is May.

The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months. This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.

It is not unusual to still be awaiting the arrival of the first storm at this time of year. In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

#51. Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected?

Severe drought has been declared in parts of southern England after months of dry weather drove some reservoirs to exceptionally low levels.

Most of England and all of Wales were already under drought conditions after both nations' hottest summers on record, which has taken its toll on rivers, crops and nature.

Roughly 30 million people across parts of England and Wales are covered by hosepipe bans, as part of water companies' efforts to manage supplies.

So how is your area doing and are you in a drought?

"Severe drought" - the highest category - has now been declared for parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex.

It means environmental authorities will ramp up monitoring of reservoir levels, river flows and water quality, as well as carry out extra checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources.

The "severe drought" classification was introduced following the 2012 drought and this is the first time it has been implemented.

The UK government says two previous events would have met the "severe drought" classification, had it been in place. They are:

August 1976, for Devon and Yorkshire in England, and Gwent, Monmouthshire and Glamorgan in Wales

Most of England and all of Wales were already in drought, following earlier announcements by the Environment Agency (EA) and Natural Resources Wales.

Parts of north-east and north-west England are in the category below drought, called "prolonged dry weather".

There are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland.

There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle.

If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies.

The EA says that south-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century.

Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity" - when there is not enough water of sufficient quality to meet demands of people and the environment.

While conditions have improved in parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some south-eastern areas remain in the most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans - officially called "temporary use bans" - if they are not already in place.

So far, 11 UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans in 2026. This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows, and filling pools.

Ten companies are spread across central, southern and eastern parts of England, and one is in Wales.

Our three main sources of water are reservoirs, rivers and from deep underground.

A key reason why parts of southern England have entered "severe drought" is low reservoir levels.

At this time of year, the Environment Agency says it would expect England's reservoirs to be about three-quarters full, but they are just over half full on average.

Ardingly Reservoir in West Sussex and Wimbleball Reservoir in Somerset are among those at "exceptionally low" levels.

Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water says most reservoir levels in Wales are normal for the time of year.

And reservoir levels in Northern Ireland and Scotland are close to average, according to the latest available data.

Many of the UK's rivers have also been affected by the low rainfall.

Most monitored river flows in England were classed as "below normal", "notably low" or "exceptionally low" in July, according to the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH).

South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs. Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks.

Groundwater levels were generally declining in September following the prolonged dry weather.

More than half of monitored sites across the UK recorded levels considered "below normal" or lower, with levels particularly low in parts of southern England.

Water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions.

These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.

It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur.

Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.

The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.

But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation.

"A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.

But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.

In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.

And while spring and summer were relatively dry for much of the UK, winter was much wetter than usual, raising questions about how effectively water is being managed.

As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planning nine new reservoirs for England by 2050, in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.

But the EA has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control water demand - potentially including hosepipe bans - may be needed in England too.

Water companies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - which are all public bodies or non-profit - also said they were taking steps to secure future supplies.

Tell us how you're affected by the hosepipe ban.

#52. Was Neanderthal life violent? This wound suggests lethal fighting was more common

A wooden spear caused the hole in this Neanderthal shoulder blade, scientists say

A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.

They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.

From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.

The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.

Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.

The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.

A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.

"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.

Scientists have used Neanderthal remains to imagine what they could have looked like

Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.

The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.

"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."

But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.

But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.

"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.

This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.

We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.

"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.

A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.

Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.

The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.

For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.

But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.

The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.

The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#53. £15m for zero-emission testing at Belfast Harbour

Testing technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption

Belfast Harbour is to become a live environment for testing zero-emission transport and energy systems.

It comes after a £15m investment from UK Research and Innovation's Local Innovation Partnerships Fund.

The cluster led by Artemis Technologies, will connect electric vessels, high-power marine charging, autonomous transport and energy systems through secure digital twin technology.

Testing these technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption.

Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use

Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use.

"What does that mean for most people? It means your bus turns up at the right time in terms of transport.

"But in terms of energy it means, more significantly that when the wind is blowing too hard, the network tells our boat 'take the power' and ultimately as we build up, it tells Belfast Harbour which uses a huge amount of energy 'take that energy'.

"Equally when the wind doesn't blow, it says 'don't use that energy' and what does that mean?

"It means we don't have to shut down windfarms and ultimately lower energy prices," he added.

Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said it will be "developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the Harbour"

This is the second project announced from the £30m allocation to the Belfast-Derry Innovation Corridor.

Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said: "It will be developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the harbour, which is a really big user.

"We are really world leading in terms of this so it is a really good investment," she added.

It's hoped what is learned in this project could have wider applications across Northern Ireland.

Dr Percy said: "Where the real accelerator value add comes in here, what can be done on that network can be rinse and repeat anywhere else."

"We already have real buy in from Foyle Port and other regions within Northern Ireland," he added.

#54. Sheep are disappearing from our hills - and our dinner plates

Sheep are disappearing from our hills - and our dinner plates

For four generations, Neil Heseltine's family have worked on Hill Top Farm, perched on the hillside of Malhamdale amid the dramatic landscape of the Yorkshire Dales. And for most of that time, sheep were the mainstay of the business.

But, Neil says, over the past 20 years there has been "a complete turnaround" and he has shifted away from sheep farming to stay afloat. In that time the 1,500-acre farm has gone from a peak of over 800 lambing sheep to just 45 this spring.

"I dread to think where the farm would have been financially had we not started to make those changes," he tells me. "I either continued along the sheep-farming route because of sentimentality or made bold decisions."

While most upland farmers still keep sheep on their land, the changes here have been mirrored across not just the Dales but the entire British farming industry. The shepherd's life has never been an easy one, but for many it's getting tougher and more difficult than ever to make a profit.

Neil Heseltine's family have worked on Hill Top Farm for four generations

The average British farmer is 60 years old, according to the National Farmers' Union (NFU), and prices for everything from fuel to fodder have risen hugely for them in recent years. Meanwhile, many farmers are facing significantly reduced income from subsidies and there are worries that recent trade deals will mean increased competition from overseas.

The UK's recent trade deals with New Zealand and Australia, struck since Brexit, eliminate tariffs and give producers in both countries large quotas on the amount of lamb they can export into the UK.

There are now 14.7 million breeding ewes in the UK - the lowest figure in living memory according to Phil Stocker, chief executive of the National Sheep Association.

Overall the national flock is also falling, down to 30.4 million sheep in 2025 - numbers last seen in the mid-20th Century, when the UK population was smaller and thus the potential market for lamb and mutton reared here was much lower.

And over the last 50 years there has been a significant fall in lamb and mutton consumption according to Becky Smith, a senior analyst at the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), which represents farmers.

In 1980 the average UK household purchased 128g of sheep meat (lamb and mutton) per person, per week. In 2024 that same measure was down to 23g per person, per week.

Sheep farming has shaped the image many of us have when we picture somewhere like the Dales with drystone walls to keep livestock enclosed and green, rolling hills kept short by seasonal grazing.

But any desire to protect the heritage of one of the UK's oldest agricultural industries is rubbing up against not just a diminishing appetite for sheep meat but also the question of whether some of our uplands might be better used to promote nature recovery and biodiversity.

All this raises the question of whether we have passed "peak sheep" in the UK - and, in turn, what that might mean for consumers. Will my children still be eating our lamb for their Sunday roast or in their baltis and bhunas in 25 years time?

And, what will happen to some of our most revered and beloved landscapes like the Lake District, Yorkshire Dales, Scottish Highlands and Welsh mountains, and the people who live and work there?

At Craven Cattle Mart on the outskirts of Skipton, North Yorkshire, the auction ring is buzzing as farmers from across the Yorkshire Dales and Pennine Moors come to buy and sell livestock.

To an outsider, business might look brisk - but general manager Jeremy Eaton says it's nowhere near as busy as when he started in the industry 47 years ago.

"We'd have some sales at this market where we'd regularly be selling 19,000 store lambs," he says. "Now we're fortunate if we get to 8,000 or 9,000."

At Craven Cattle Marts, farmers come from across the Yorkshire Dales and Pennine Moors to buy and sell livestock

People who work sheep know that it's some of the hardest farming there is. A former shepherd once told me that sheep are only ever trying to do one of three things: "Escape, or die, or escape and then immediately die."

Globally, lamb consumption is expected to grow by 15% between now and 2032, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the Food and Agriculture Organization.

But changing tastes in the UK mean mutton, made from mature sheep, is no longer eaten in the same volume it was by previous generations and lamb has seemingly gone from a weekly staple to a meat more often eaten on special occasions, with "white meat" like chicken being increasingly chosen over lamb and beef.

The drop in the national flock has actually led to robust growth in the price paid for lamb according to Becky Smith from the AHDB, with the sheep price hitting record highs in 2024.

But despite the higher price for their sheep, upland farmers with tight margins feel the pinch more than many when diesel and oil costs go up. And on top of that, the cost of feeding sheep has also rocketed - the average cost of a bale of hay is £155 a tonne this spring compared to £75 a tonne this time last year.

There are now 14.7 million breeding ewes in the UK, according to the National Sheep Association

Farmers and groups such as Compassion in World Farming have also raised concerns that new trade deals could undermine UK agriculture because farms here must meet high welfare standards that may not be not required in several partner countries.

Extremely tight margins mean growing numbers of younger people can't see a future in farming.

This is immediately apparent as you wander around Craven Cattle Marts. "You can see here today, most of the generation of farmers are over 60," says Hayley Baines, a 39-year-old sheep farmer from Gisburn in the Ribble Valley. "There [aren't] many young ones because there's better options."

And some welcome the decline in sheep farming.

"Fewer sheep means less suffering […] a sheep's life in the wool and mutton industries belies our reputation as a nation of animal lovers," says Mimi Bekhechi, senior vice president at the UK's People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta).

The UK's Climate Change Committee has also previously advised the government to encourage people to cut the amount of meat and dairy they consume, to combat climate change.

Matthew Cole of the NFU says a further issue has been the move - especially post-Brexit - away from farmers receiving paid subsidies from the EU either for the volume of livestock they have or amount of land they farm.

In their place, successive UK governments have introduced new schemes with a stronger focus on farming for nature - meaning many farmers are facing significantly reduced subsidy income.

For example the Westminster government's Sustainable Farming Incentive scheme, which was updated last month, includes further incentives for farmers in England to graze moorland with cattle and ponies instead of sheep as it "contributes positively to biodiversity". Cattle, for example, do not graze as low to the ground as sheep, allowing smaller plants to flower.

UK governments have introduced new schemes with a stronger focus on farming for nature

Neil Heseltine of Hill Top Farm now has 300 cattle who graze outside all year round, a shift that he says has made the farm more profitable and dramatically reduced the hours he has to put into it.

But while these new subsidy schemes are welcomed in principle by many farmers, some find the funding available falls far short of the levels provided under earlier support systems.

"Going forward, do I see a future? I'm not sure where we're going with it," says James Foster, who has been farming beef and sheep on the Bolton Abbey Estate for 30 years. "I do believe the government don't want us, but people have to eat and we just have to adapt with that."

Defra says that an average of £2.3bn a year is being invested through its farming schemes in England and insists it is protecting farmers in trade deals and also making supply chains fairer.

Today, Scottish sheep and upland farmers face many of the same challenges of tighter margins, rising costs and falling appetite for lamb and mutton and the Holyrood government have likewise tried to move towards a subsidy regime which gives greater weight to the environmental benefits farmers can provide. One example is the "Sheep and Trees" initiative which aims to help farmers and land managers plant more woodlands without cutting the size of their flock.

There have been complaints from farmers that some of the schemes introduced in Scotland have not been easy enough to access, leading the Agriculture Minister Jim Farlie to commit to reviewing certain projects. At the start of this year NFU Scotland and other farming organisations also raised concerns that the amount of government money budgeted to support agriculture was not enough either to support farmers to profitably make food or to help them meet climate and nature goals.

In Northern Ireland, the sheep population has fallen for several years with the most recent stats from 2024 showing 1.9 million sheep across the region. The Ulster Farmers Union has criticised the exclusion of sheep farmers from the devolved administration's future agriculture policy and called on Northern Ireland's Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs to engage with the industry.

Sheep were first domesticated approximately 10,500 years ago in the Middle East, and were eventually brought to British shores by Neolithic farmers some time around 4000BC. Sheep became such an important part of the landscape that by medieval times the phrase, "half the wealth of England rides on the back of the sheep" became familiar.

In Scotland, sheep have also played a pivotal role in the rural economy for generations and Scotland's sheep population there has been more stable in recent years at around 6.5 million.

The history of Scottish sheep farming is also indelibly tied up with the controversial Highland Clearances when, in the late-18th and 19th century, traditional crofting families, were moved off the land when landowners realised they could make more money from farming sheep than leasing their land.

In 2004, sheep were removed from the limestone landscapes of Ingleborough, the second-highest mountain in the Yorkshire Dales and replaced with roaming native cattle breeds, who are less intensive grazers as part of the Wild Ingleborough project.

"Going forward, do I see a future? I'm not sure where we're going with it," says James Foster (right)

Two new scientific studies published in the academic journal Ecological Solutions and Evidence, show the huge impact that change has had for nature across the 1500-hectare landscape, with plant diversity increased by over 40% and a five-fold increase in the number of butterflies in the absence of sheep.

Robyn Wrigley, from the University of Leeds School of Earth and Environment, co-authored both studies and says the research provides long-term evidence of how different grazing impacts biodiversity and can help inform discussions about restoration.

Neil Heseltine of Hill Top Farm now has 300 cattle who graze outside all year round

These changes, however, are not ones that all farmers welcome. Some I spoke to look at the landscape and see only lost livestock pasture and question how their way of life and livelihoods fit into such a future.

But David Stanners, Uplands North Group Chair at the NFU, says it's possible for the rewilding lobby and the farmers to find common ground.

"To understand better what Natural England wants from the uplands, what wildlife trusts want, they need to understand what we (the farmers) want," he says. "There needs to be compromise and respect on all sides."

But there is a ray of sunshine for the industry, according to Phil Stocker from the National Sheep Association. He believes the domestic market for sheep meat is going to keep driving forward, in large part thanks to demand from the increasing number of Muslim people in the UK.

AHDB statistics suggest that 80% of halal consumers eat lamb on a weekly basis and 64% eat mutton weekly. By contrast, only 6% of the general UK population eats lamb each week.

According to the AHDB, while Muslims make up around 6.5% of the UK population they account for 30% of lamb sales annually. Lamb is often Muslim consumers' meat of choice for family occasions and festivals like Ramadan and Eid, while mutton is a popular ingredient in curries and stews.

Because of this, Stocker says he doesn't envisage the total demise of the industry. But right now, he adds, "we're surviving by people's interest and by market demand almost in spite of the work that the policy makers and others are doing on agricultural and land management policy".

Most upland farmers still keep sheep on their land

A worst-case scenario for farmers and consumers would see UK lamb become even more expensive and less common on our shelves in favour of ever more sheep meat imported from major suppliers like New Zealand and Australia.

The AHDB project sheep are likely to decrease in number across many farms but take a walk in the Lake District or Welsh mountains in another 25 years and you will likely still see sheep dotting the hillsides.

Farmers and conservationists alike told me they need to see clear plans for what policymakers want from the uplands for the next generation. Their hope is that, as we move into the second quarter of the 21st Century, traditional sheep farmers and rewilders alike find their place in the nation's cherished uplands.

Top picture credit: Universal Images Group via Getty Images

Correction 15 October: This article was amended to make clear that the Sustainable Farming Incentive and the £2.3bn a year Defra investment apply only to England, not England and Wales as we reported. When it was first published the article mentioned the SFI but did not make clear where it was available. It was updated shortly afterwards to say it applied to England and Wales but this has now been corrected to state it only applies to England.

#55. Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says

Flooding in the Kucukcekmece district of Istanbul

Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported.

A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement.

Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts.

Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut Gül to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.

The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted.

Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue.

Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding.

"I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X.

He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time.

The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said.

A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks.

More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces.

In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave.

#56. 'Nowhere to escape' - Indonesians share footage of orange haze blanketing towns

A thick orange smog has descended on the Indonesian city of Palangka Raya.

Witnesses captured videos of the haze washing over the Kalimantan region not far from where wildfires continue to burn.

The ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200, according to data from the national environment ministry, four times higher than the "hazardous" level of 300 on Wednesday.

Toxic smog is choking millions across Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia, with authorities partly blaming the agricultural clearing method known as "slash and burn" for compounding the intense haze.

#57. Dog that hunts invasive 'sea vomit' honoured as animal of the year

A working dog from the Scottish Highlands has been named animal of the year by a charity for hunting down an invasive marine creature called the carpet sea squirt.

This organism, also nicknamed "sea vomit", is particularly harmful to coastal wildlife and economies.

Working at low tide with her owner, Dr Texa Sim, black Labrador Sgiath has found hundreds of colonies of the sea squirt, which - if left uncontrolled - can smother and kill native species.

Sgiath (pronounced Skee-ah) is thought to be the UK's first sea squirt-hunting dog.

Carpet sea squirt can be tricky to spot among seaweed

The International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) , external is awarding Sgiath animal of the years at its 26th annual animal Action Awards ceremony on Thursday 15 October.

Sim, a marine ecologist based near Glencoe, has had Sgiath since she was a puppy and the bond between the two is strong.

"Sgiath is incredibly clever. Her problem solving and her ability to take on new challenges and learn so quickly are just phenomenal, and it's so amazing to watch."

As a pup, Sgiath was trained as a mountain rescue dog. The Labrador proved to be so good that Sim wondered if she could use her skills to help with marine conservation work.

Sgiath has been trained to recognise the scent of the carpet sea squirt. And now, the six year old joins her owner on the beaches to sniff it out.

Sim says the dog is always right when pointing out a sea squirt, which can be difficult to spot, looking like slime among seaweed and on structures like pontoons and oyster cages.

Carpet sea squirt, or sea vomit, has spread to several places around the UK

"When I first started this project, I genuinely didn't know whether it would work," said Sim.

"No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackle this problem in the marine environment. It began as a proof-of-concept project and has exceeded every expectation I had."

Dogs' scent detection skills are often used in conservation work on land, including tracking endangered species and helping investigate environmental crime. At low tide, Sgiath can, as Sim puts it "dive down under the seaweed".

"She just does a survey with her nose, essentially, she can pinpoint exactly where it is, so it's much easier," she said.

Marine experts believe that carpet sea squirt, formally named Didemnum vexillum, came from Japan. It arrived on the shores of the south of England and Wales in 2008.

It can appear in various shades - from orange to cream - and has now spread to several seaside locations across the UK.

It reproduces quickly during the warmer summer months and, with warming seas, there are fears it could spread further.

Dr Martyn Kurr, a marine biologist from Bangor University told BBC News that non-native or "biofouling" species, like the carpet sea squirt, can outcompete native wildlife for valuable nutrients.

"These species also clog up aquaculture pens, marine infrastructure, and machinery such as boat propellors," he explained.

Efforts to control and clean up these problematic marine invaders costs millions of pounds every year across Europe.

Sgiath is also a trained mountain rescue dog

To get Sgiarth proficient in both mountain rescue and marine conservation has needed hard work and long hours from both dog and owner.

To locate and draw attention to a lost hiker on mountainous terrain, Sgiath is trained to bark and bounce around.

Conservation work requires a quieter approach.

Sim explained that she trains Sgiath to give what's known as a "passive indication" when she finds the sea squirt.

"It's a kind of a stillness, or a stare."

Sgiath has been trained to stare when she finds carpet sea squirt

When we speak to Sim over Zoom from her home, her two dogs are curled up in their beds at her feet. Apparently, when Sgiath is not out finding lost people or marine creatures, she likes to be wrapped up in her dog blanket.

Sgiath, and Sim's younger Labrador Uisage, are both working dogs that are driven to do their jobs with treats and play.

Kurr, from Bangor University, said that scientists were just starting to realise that "these wonderful animals can smell changes in water that signal a marine invasion which otherwise might have gone unnoticed".

He added: "It's fantastic to see Sgiath get this much deserved award, and I'm very excited to see what other wonderful work we can do with sniffer dogs."

#58. India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats

The recent floods in Nepal have highlighted the need for cross-border co-operation in the Himalayan region

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August.

But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention.

Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions.

"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said.

A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage.

"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said.

Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment.

But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes?

India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control.

But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat.

Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods.

Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important.

Balendra Shah has urged neighbours India and China to collaborate on climate risks in the Himalayan region

A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period.

Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online.

Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau.

The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily.

A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms.

While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau.

The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress.

The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations.

Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas.

In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet.

Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project.

Hundreds of people were killed in the deadly flood that tore through the China-Nepal border in August

But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort.

"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute.

"What happened after that no one knows," he added.

Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet.

But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022.

China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said.

Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes.

"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group.

But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved.

One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value.

"What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank.

Experts have raised concerns over climate-related risks as the Himalayan snow cover melts rapidly

Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders.

The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow.

"There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD.

He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks.

Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay.

"Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says.

Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain.

For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

#59. Suspected fly tippers shamed with online photos

The council said it had received thousands of comments on the social media posts from residents who had also "had enough" of fly tipping

A west London council that says it has "had enough" of fly tipping has begun sharing CCTV images on social media, showing people allegedly being caught in the act of dumping rubbish in public places.

Hillingdon Council described the crime as a "blight" on the borough, and as a local authority, it had "allowed the problem to get bigger".

Cabinet member for community environment and enforcement, Adam Bennett, said the action was a "really good first step" adding: "We really need to up our game on all forms of of enforcement."

He said since its CCTV images were shared earlier this week they had over 850,000 views, received 2,500 comments including information on who the perpetrators might be.

Hillingdon Council's enforcement teams have identified a hotspot outside the car park for St Anselm's Church in Hayes

Bennett said the reaction to the posts showed fly tipping was "a really important issue to residents".

Hillingdon Council says it issues a £1,000 fixed penalty fine to culprits, and last month it seized and crushed a vehicle that was linked to fly tipping.

"We've had enough as have residents, of the very small minority of individuals who choose to blight our neighbourhoods and communities by thinking it's acceptable to just dump their waste here on the pavement, on a verge, or on a lay-by."

He said by sharing images of suspects' faces the council was "taking action to try and bring the perpetrators to account".

Bennett added: "If you see your face on social media or perhaps on one of our screens in our libraries, our leisure centres, you're going to think twice about wanting to fly tip again."

Bennett explained that "a certain evidential threshold" had to be reached before identifying individuals online, but said as a council they did not want to "shy away" from the problem.

"If you're going to do it in Hillingdon, we're going to call you out for it, and we're going to take every opportunity we can to penalise you for what is unlawful environmental crime that blights the lives of our communities and all of the hard-working taxpayers in this country."

The council said images like this would be shared on their social media platforms as well as on screens in libraries and leisure centres, to identify individuals

Liberal Democrat London Assembly committee member Gareth Roberts said he was "interested" to see if Hillingdon's tactics of "naming and shaming" individuals worked to prevent fly tipping.

"We need to use everything at our disposal to make sure that we clamp down on these people who think that they can simply trash London because they're too lazy to take things to the appropriate recycling or dumping sites," he said.

This week, City Hall's Environment Committee looked at how London boroughs are responding to the problem of fly tipping, as well as the overall coordination of the response to it.

Roberts said fly tipping is a "major problem" for London and explained there were nearly half a million incidents, across the capital, last year alone.

"Unfortunately clearing up this mess costs councils money and it costs Londoners money," he said.

"What we need is governments to recognise that there is a particular problem in London. We have more fly tipping than anywhere else and it would be great if they could find a way to give councils the money and the resources and the powers to tackle this scourge which is blighting parts of London."
